item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q022_colg_crya_remote_homology","answer":"In SCOPe 2.04, the ColG collagen-binding domain d1nqda_ and the Cry3A C-terminal domain d1dlca3 were classified separately, so SCOPe did not assert a superfamily-level evolutionary relationship. In current SCOPe (release 2.08), they are grouped in the same collagen-binding-domain-like superfamily, while remaining different families. This upgrades their relationship from structural resemblance without an explicit homology claim to probable remote common ancestry—not close family-level homology. The principal evidence is their conserved compact antiparallel beta-sandwich/jelly-roll core, including corresponding strand topology, packing, and three-dimensional alignment despite weak sequence similarity. Their functions are also compatible at a broad level: d1nqda_ is a noncatalytic ColG targeting module that binds collagen, whereas d1dlca3 is the Cry3A receptor-recognition/specificity domain and can participate in glycan or midgut-receptor binding; Cry3A pore formation is performed principally by other domains. Thus both are appended bacterial surface-recognition modules, although this functional analogy alone would not prove ancestry. The common superfamily does not justify transferring collagen binding to Cry3A, insecticidal activity to ColG, or detailed ligand specificity between them. Either structure can guide a remote structural template for the conserved beta-sandwich core, but loops and binding surfaces require independent structural or biochemical evidence; neither domain should be chosen as a functional representative of the other family merely because SCOPe now unites them at superfamily level.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
